name: Mada / Maɗa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Ernst-Kurdi, Eszter. 2017. The Phonology of Mada. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon (Ministry of Scientific Research and Innovation), 63 pp. [SIL archive 76424]. Corroborating: Nkoumou, Hubert Fernand. 2003. Esquisse phonologique, alphabet et principes orthographiques du Mada. Mémoire de Maîtrise, Université de Yaoundé I, v+162 pp.
catalog_locator: Ernst-Kurdi 2017 §2.6 'Metrical structure', p. 56; also §2.1 p. 9, §2.5 'Tone' p. 50, §2.6.2 p. 57, §3 'Conclusion' p. 59. Nkoumou 2003 §2.3.5.3.1 p. 66 (p. 75) and ch. 3 §3.1.1-3.1.2 p. 78 (p. 87).
catalog_quote: [Ernst-Kurdi 2017, p. 56] Stress is challenging to determine phonetically. In the case of Mada, stressed syllables contain a full vowel as well as have a higher pitch and increased volume. Stress is not a feature of the word. Native speakers perceive stress as ‘the rhythm of the language’ which is essential to the correct way of speaking. Rhythmic stress in Mada runs from right to left and is right-headed. Feet consist of two to three syllables. In other words, starting from the right, the last syllable of a phrase is stressed and then every second or third syllable as well. ... Mada prefers iambic (weak-strong) or anapaestic (weak-weak-strong) foot structures. Strong syllables are usually closed syllables and/or carry high tone. There seems to be a correlation between stressed syllables and high tone, but more research is needed in the future in order to establish the complex rules that govern and influence stress in Mada. [p. 59] Mada is a tonal language, it has two level tones: High and Low. ... Mada has a metrical stress pattern. Rhythmic stress runs from right to left and is right-headed. Iambic or anapaestic foot structures are preferred. [Nkoumou 2003, p. 66] La voyelle affectée doit être en finale de mot et comme celle-ci porte l’accent final de la parler dans la position isolée. [p. 78] Il y a trois tons simples en Maɗa: HAUT (v́) [ndáɗ] «droit» MOYEN (v̄) [ndaɗ] «appetit» BAS (v̀) [ndàɗ] «poignée/déraciner»
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: [p. 66] La voyelle affectée doit être en finale de mot et comme celle-ci porte l'accent final de la parler dans la position isolée. [p. 78] En général, il s'agit d'un système de niveaux de tons simples. Trois tons de base, Haut, Moyen et Bas. Les tons modulés existent dans la langue Maɗa, mais sont traités comme une séquence de niveaux de tons. [...] Il y a trois tons simples en Maɗa : HAUT (v́) [ndáɗ] «droit» MOYEN (v̄) [ndāɗ] «appetit» BAS (v̀) [ndàɗ] «poignée/déraciner»
new_statements.translation: [p. 66] The affected vowel must be word-final and, as such, carries the final accent of the utterance in isolated position. [p. 78] In general it is a system of simple level tones. Three basic tones: High, Mid and Low. Contour tones exist in Mada but are treated as a sequence of tone levels. [...] There are three simple tones in Mada: HIGH [ndáɗ] 'straight/right', MID [ndāɗ] 'appetite', LOW [ndàɗ] 'handful / to uproot'.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (171 PDF pages, Acrobat Capture scan with scanned layer) via the rendered page scan pages/book p. 66) and pages/book p. 78). p. 66, §2.3.5.3.1 'Réduction ou effacement', reads exactly as quoted: 'Aucun mot isolé en Maɗa ne contient le [ə] phonétique.. La voyelle affectée doit être en finale de mot et comme celle-ci porte l'accent final de la parler dans la position isolée.' (a handwritten correction mark sits over 'de la' but the printed text is as quoted); the paragraph then continues 'En Muyang, le [j] de [-aj] dans les verbes..', so the passage is indeed adapted from the Muyang analysis. p. 78, ch. 3 'Le ton' §3.1.1-3.1.2, matches verbatim ('En général, il s'agit d'un système de n…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mada is described as a three-level tone language (H, M, L; no contour tones; tone mostly grammatical, few lexical minimal pairs). No word-stress system is described. The single stress-like remark says that a word pronounced in isolation carries a 'final accent' on its last vowel (which is why that vowel resists the reduction to [ə]/deletion it undergoes medially in connected speech) - i.e. phrase-final prominence on the final syllable of citation forms, not a lexical stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. For tone: informant reports tones on syllabic nasals/consonants (p. 78 remark, 'to be studied'); Ernst-Kurdi 2017 (p. 18) recognises only two tone levels (high, low) against Nkoumou's three.
new_statements.domain_note: The p. 66 remark concerns isolated (citation-form) words vs. word-medial position inside an utterance ('émission de parler'); it is phrase-final, not word-level, and the paragraph is modelled on the Muyang analysis (it continues 'En Muyang..'), so it may be a carried-over generalisation rather than a Mada-specific observation.
new_statements.identity_note: Both opened sources describe the Mada of the Mada massif / canton Madakalkoss, arrondissement of Tokombéré, Mayo-Sava (Nkoumou's data collected there 2001-2002); no dialect split is made. Not to be confused with Mada of Nigeria (Plateau, ISO mda). The earlier scan named only the unreachable Barreteau & Brunet 2000 dictionary; the MA thesis it missed is open at the MPI Language Description Heritage archive.

tone_statements.citation: Ernst-Kurdi, Eszter. 2017. The Phonology of Mada. Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon / Ministry of Scientific Research and Innovation, 63 pp. [SIL Language & Culture Archives 76424].
tone_statements.quote: [p. 50] Barreteau and Brunet (2000, p. 41) as well as Nkoumou (2003, p. 81) describe Mada as having three level tones, however they admit that with further analysis it might be possible to reduce the number of tones to two. [p. 51] The new analysis offered here takes into consideration the pitch-lowering effect of depressor consonants and therefore posits that Mada has only two underlying tones, even if phonetically speaking three level tones can be observed. The depressor consonants in Mada are all the voiced obstruents and they lower the pitch of adjacent vowels. [...] Tone carries a relatively low lexical load as there are only a few minimal pairs found in the data.
tone_statements.n_tones: 2 underlying (H, L); 3 phonetic levels via depressor lowering

tone_statements.citation: Ernst-Kurdi, Eszter. 2016. Tense, Aspect and Mood in Mada, a Central-Chadic Language. M.A. dissertation, Redcliffe College (University of Gloucestershire); issued Yaoundé: SIL Cameroon / Ministry of Scientific Research and Innovation, 125 pp. [SIL Cameroon Language & Culture Archives 76492].
tone_statements.quote: A preliminary analysis conducted by the author on the tone patterns of Mada nouns and verbs, taking into account the pitch lowering effects of depressor consonants, has indicated that Mada may only have two underlying tones: High and Low. The underlying Low tone can be further lowered by the effect of depressor consonants which explains why phonetically speaking three surface tones can be distinguished. The depressor consonants in Mada are all voiced obstruents. They lower the pitch of adjacent vowels with Low tones to be realised as super low in both open and closed syllables.

sources.note: Full phonology (prosodies, consonants, vowels, tone ch. 3 pp. 78-99, syllable ch. 4 pp. 100-105). Three level tones H/M/L, no contour tones (p. 78). Only stress-like remark: in vowel-reduction section p. 66 the word-final vowel 'porte l'accent final.. dans la position isolée' (final accent in isolated/citation position). No word-stress rule; 'accent' elsewhere only as orthographic tone marks (p. 123).
